src/mesh/topology.ts also exports: MeshTopology { version, vertexCount, landmarkIndices (readonly (number|null)[], length 37, null only at the centroid), triangles (readonly (readonly [number,number,number])[]) }. Triangles are generated (NOT hand-typed, NOT a Delaunay/triangulation library) by a small zigzag(innerRingVertexIds, outerRingVertexIds) helper applied to (inner ring, outer lip ring) and (outer lip ring, boundary ring), plus a fan(centroidVertexId, innerRingVertexIds) helper closing the inner ring -- see the reference zigzag/fan implementation sketch below. Expected output: 24 + 24 + 12 = 60 triangles. Export DEFAULT_TOPOLOGY as a module-level frozen constant and TOPOLOGY_VERSION = 1. Add a Vitest snapshot test (src/mesh/topology.test.ts) asserting DEFAULT_TOPOLOGY.triangles matches a snapshot, following the existing test style in src/align/transform.test.ts and src/align/region.test.ts.

Reference zigzag/fan sketch (adapt as needed, keep it this simple -- do not introduce a general polygon triangulation): function zigzag(inner: readonly number[], outer: readonly number[]) pairs same-length rings index-by-index with wraparound (i, i+1 mod n) producing 2 triangles per ring step; function fan(centre: number, ring: readonly number[]) produces one triangle per ring step from the centre vertex to consecutive ring points with wraparound.

New module src/mesh/geometry.ts exports: CONTROL_REFERENCE_POSE = { jawOpen: 'BIG_OPEN', lipWidth: 'WIDE', lipRound: 'ROUND', lipClosure: 'CLOSED' } as const satisfies Record<string, MouthPose>; PoseMeshGeometry { pose: MouthPose, points: readonly Point[] } (length 37, avatar pixel space); async extractPoseGeometry(frame: ImageBitmap, topology: MeshTopology): Promise<PoseMeshGeometry | null> -- runs detect() from src/align/landmarks.ts on the frame, returns null on faceCount !== 1 or no landmarks (mirror the existing soft-failure pattern in src/align/quality.ts's checkCapture, do not throw), otherwise maps each of the confirmed MediaPipe indices (plus the synthetic centroid) onto topology vertex ids in the frame's own pixel space; AvatarMeshGeometry { topologyVersion: number, restPoints: readonly Point[], deltas: Partial<Record<MouthPose, readonly Point[]>> }; async computeAvatarMeshGeometry(avatar: Pick<Avatar,'frames'>, topology?: MeshTopology): Promise<AvatarMeshGeometry> -- runs extractPoseGeometry against avatar.frames.REST plus whichever of CLOSED/BIG_OPEN/WIDE/ROUND avatar.frames has, computes REST-relative deltas for each detected pose (points[i] - restPoints[i]) and omits a pose's delta entirely if avatar.frames lacks it or extraction returned null. Apply a per-vertex deadzone: snap any delta with magnitude below interOcularDistance(restLandmarks) * 0.01 to exactly {x:0,y:0} (reuse or mirror interOcularDistance's approach from src/align/quality.ts). Add src/mesh/geometry.test.ts covering: deadzone snapping, a pose's absence producing no delta entry, and extractPoseGeometry returning null on a detection with faceCount 0 (mock the detect() import).

New module src/mesh/solver.ts exports: MeshControls { jawOpen: number, lipWidth: number, lipRound: number, lipClosure: number } (deliberately a subset of core/articulation.ts's Articulation -- no tongue in this milestone); MeshTarget { points: readonly Point[] } (length 37); solveMeshTarget(controls: MeshControls, geometry: AvatarMeshGeometry, topology: MeshTopology): MeshTarget -- computes target = restPoints + SUM over the four controls of (control value clamped 0..1) * (geometry.deltas[CONTROL_REFERENCE_POSE[control]] ?? zero vector). This is an additive weighted SUM of independent per-control deltas, explicitly NOT nearest-pose averaging or interpolation between only two poses. clampMeshTarget(target: MeshTarget, geometry: AvatarMeshGeometry): MeshTarget -- for each vertex, clamps the combined displacement-from-rest vector's magnitude to the largest single-pose delta magnitude ever observed for that vertex across geometry.deltas (so e.g. jawOpen=1 AND lipClosure=1 together cannot displace a vertex further than the single most extreme reference photo did). solveMeshTarget must call clampMeshTarget internally before returning. Add src/mesh/solver.test.ts covering: a single control at 1.0 reproduces that pose's exact geometry (rest + its delta), two controls at 0.5 sum roughly additively, and an extreme combination is clamped rather than unbounded.

notes:
This work order is milestone 1 of a larger, explicitly gated multi-milestone plan (full context in DESIGN_DECISIONS.md's existing 2026-09-07 'Continuous articulation over five reference frames (Stage 1)' entry, which this milestone continues as 'Stage 2'). The whole point of this milestone is a human visually judging the mesh deformation before speech integration is attempted, so do not proceed to wiring this into LipSyncPlayer/timeline/TTS regardless of how well it seems to be going -- that is a deliberate, human-gated later milestone, not an oversight to fix opportunistically.

Why the design is this specific: the current renderer alpha-crossfades two whole baked photographs, which moves jaw, chin, cheeks, skin texture and lighting together and reads as photos being swapped rather than a face speaking. The prior Stage 1 entry in DESIGN_DECISIONS.md already pre-committed to geometric landmark warping as the real fix and already settled the one hard constraint: raw pose photos are deleted after baking for privacy, so geometry must be recovered by re-detecting landmarks on the baked (already rigidly aligned) frames. That decision is settled -- do not relitigate it or try to preserve raw photos.

The delta-sum solver (rather than nearest-pose blending) is deliberate: geometric deltas do not ghost the way alpha-blended photographs do, so summing roughly independent articulators (a jaw drop co-occurring with lip widening) is the correct model, and it is what lets jaw and lips finally move at different speeds -- the specific defect Stage 1 could not fix, because with welded frames jaw and lips are literally the same pixels.

The boundary (jaw/cheek) ring deliberately is NOT pinned to zero motion. Its per-pose deltas are measured from the user's own baked BIG_OPEN/CLOSED/WIDE/ROUND photographs, and a movable chin is the entire point of this stage. What keeps the upper face immobile is that no mesh triangle reaches it -- the rigid landmarks (eye corners, nose bridge) stay outside the mesh entirely, used only for the existing whole-avatar registration as they are today. Do not add a pinning mechanism inside the mesh.

After you have settled the approach, you may delegate bounded mechanical sub-work to a lower-cost worker rather than doing it yourself -- the three test files (src/mesh/topology.test.ts, src/mesh/solver.test.ts, src/mesh/warp.test.ts) are the plausible candidates once their contracts are fixed, and only if that is actually cheaper than writing them inline. Write a work order as JSON (task, requirements, constraints, startingPoints, validation, plus complexity / bounded / exploration / risk / expectedCost) and run: node ~/.claude/workers/bin/delegate.js <order.json> --controller codex --json. The router decides whether a cheaper worker is available and affordable and returns the result; if it routes back to you, just do the work -- that is ordinary routing, not a bypass, so no --worker flag is needed either way. Inspect the resulting diff and validation output yourself before continuing -- delegated work is yours to verify. Keep the landmark-index verification, the geometry/solver maths, and the canvas warp renderer in your own hands; those are the subtle parts. Never call Qwen or Gemini directly; the router is the only path down.
